sections.title: Nineteen years between the interface and the code that ships it.
sections.text: I am a Product Designer and Front-End Engineer based in Madrid. I studied journalism (Ciencias de la Información) at the Universidad Complutense and then graphic design at Escuela Arteneo — which is probably why my work keeps returning to editorial problems: hierarchy, reading rhythm, and how much meaning survives when a layout gets compressed. I started in an agency in 2007, building sites for clients like Barceló Viajes and Vodafone. Then nine years at France Telecom Spain on high-traffic products, optimising flows and conversion structures. In 2021 I moved fully into design systems at Aliseda, where I created Brickee, their internal system. Since 2023 I have been at Prensa Ibérica working on 42DS: design-token architecture from Figma to Style Dictionary, WCAG 2.1 AA in complex editorial products, and the shared SCSS architecture behind the group's titles.

pages.title: 42DS — Multi-brand design system · José Luis Pizarro
pages.headline: 42DS — From shared foundations to an AI-operable design system.
pages.description: Prensa Ibérica had fourteen brand setups and a business that could not stop while they were unified. 42DS is the architecture underneath: 97% shared SCSS against 3% brand configuration, and later a system AI could read.

sections.title: A small in-house team, and a share of it that can be counted.
sections.text: 42DS is built and maintained by a small in-house team. It is not one person’s system, and reading the rest of this case as though it were would be wrong. I joined mainly as a designer and front-end profile inside an architecture other people had already started, and my part grew with it: as of August 2026, 6,637 of the repository’s 11,622 commits since February 2023 are mine. That is the most honest way I have of saying how much of this is my work and how much is not. Below are the people I worked with most closely — and the commit count measures code, so not everyone whose decisions shaped the system appears in it. Juan Francisco Molinera Product Design Lead LinkedIn Susana Cabado Design System Engineer LinkedIn Jorge Herrero Chief Product Officer LinkedIn Act 01 What had to be decided

sections.title: Unify without stopping the company.
sections.text: Prensa Ibérica had grown into a multi-brand ecosystem with different technologies, identities and legacy decisions. Unification had to happen while BAU work — fixes, sponsorships, visual changes and editorial requests — continued. So the first job was not “design the new system”. It was understand the existing one: audit performance and CSS complexity, learn the legacy and identify what could become shared.

sections.title: One fix, every brand.
sections.text: The bar was a behaviour rather than a number, and it is worth stating both halves of it. What success looked like A correction made once reaching every title, and a new brand arriving as configuration instead of as code. If the same fix still had to be repeated per masthead, the system had not done its job whatever it looked like. What nobody measured No one wrote that bar down or tracked it against a baseline. This was business as usual with a system growing inside it, so the evidence is structural — the shared/brand split and the fourteen setups — and not a before-and-after.

sections.title: Separate what is global from what is brand-specific.
sections.text: I drew the line by what a brand can redefine, not by where the code lives. Four of the five layers are shared. Only the brand setup changes. Measured today, that split is 97% shared SCSS against 3% brand configuration: fourteen brand setups, six for web and eight for AMP. Shared by every brand ABSTRACTS variables mixins maps functions BASE reset helpers dark LAYOUT grid breakpoints FOURTIES atoms molecules organisms internal package name Per brand BRANDS setup typography colour behaviours Shared foundations first. Brand configuration and component composition sit on top. Act 02 How the system is built

sections.title: One core. Multiple layers of composition and delivery.
sections.text: 42DS is easier to understand as a system of relationships: foundations feed reusable components, brand configuration changes expression, and production targets consume the same shared logic.

sections.title: Small primitives become editorial products.
sections.text: The hierarchy communicates scale without treating Atomic Design as dogma. Lower-level primitives are composed into increasingly contextual product patterns. 05 Product patterns 04 Organisms 03 Molecules 02 Atoms 01 Foundations

sections.title: A component is a contract, not just a drawing.
sections.text: Each piece connects design intent, reusable structure and implementation behaviour. This makes the hand-off understandable to both designers and developers. media category · metadata Headline becomes reusable content structure Optional supporting text lives inside the same semantic component. byline / time atom molecule responsive accessible

sections.title: Reuse before create.
sections.text: The useful rule was not the Atomic Design label. It was the decision model: reuse first, extend when structure stays compatible, and create a new component only when semantics or architecture really change. 134 component families Three composition levels make the inventory easier to reason about and reuse. 31 Atoms 71 Molecules 32 Organisms

sections.title: One core. Different identities.
sections.text: Brand setups control typography, colour, helpers and specific behaviour. Components consume that context instead of duplicating the whole implementation. 42DS CORE SPORT sport-setup EL PERIÓDICO ep-setup EPE epe-setup REGIONALES regionales-setup REVISTAS revistas-setup

sections.title: One structure. Many identities.
sections.text: The header was a strong stress test: one information architecture and semantic structure, then brand expression through logos, typography, colour and selected variants. Shared semantic core Header architecture logo slot primary nav secondary nav actions responsive states elPeriódico News Economy Culture ☰ Identity Red · editorial same structure SPORT Football Barça Results ☰ Identity Sport red · dense nav same structure Regional Local Opinion Services ☰ Identity Blue · local news same structure Magazine Style Culture People ☰ Identity Neutral · lifestyle same structure 1 semantic DOM 1 information architecture N brand expressions WCAG 2.1 AA implemented, not aspirational Act 04 What it cost to ship

sections.title: A design system built for imperfect constraints.
sections.text: 42DS had to support parallel AMP entry points, brand bundles, paywall variants and legacy compatibility. The architecture was designed for a live business, not a clean-room rebuild. AMP is the hardest of those constraints: it caps inline CSS at 75 KB per page, and the eight AMP brand cores ship at around 33 KB — under half the ceiling. HTML5 brand cores + header extensions AMP parallel abstracts, mixins and brand setups PIANO paywall-specific core bundles LEGACY migration + compatibility while BAU continued

sections.title: The hand-off is part of the system.
sections.text: A component was not finished when it looked right in Figma. It also needed a canonical implementation, documentation and a clear path into Vue. Figma foundations · variants · states HTML / SCSS / JS canonical implementation Storybook documentation · testing · shared language Vue Tech integration Act 05 Then AI had to read it too

sections.title: Then the system had to become understandable to AI.
sections.text: What began as AI support for isolated JavaScript tasks became a portable mind-system. Each mode owns a domain; governance defines execution order and conflict resolution, so AI can work with the real 42DS rules instead of inventing around them. Source of truth 42DS knowledge components · conventions · architecture ↓ 13 specialised modes UX UI 42DS SCSS JS Storybook Docs ↓ Decision layer Governance domain ownership · execution order · conflict resolution ↓ Default principle REUSE-FIRST inspect compose extend create

sections.title: One system, several kinds of work.
sections.text: Shared patterns Design and front-end speak the same component language. Brand independence Identity changes without rebuilding the whole structure. Production paths HTML5, AMP, Piano and legacy can coexist. AI reuse Agents inspect and compose the existing system before inventing.

sections.title: The architecture grew. My role grew with it.
sections.text: My role moved toward end-to-end product design and AI-assisted execution as the system expanded. What I did not anticipate is that the decisive work would turn out to be documentary rather than visual: the line between what is shared and what belongs to a brand holds because it is written down and enforced, not because it was drawn well once. The most important evolution was not adding more components. It was turning implicit knowledge into an explicit system — first for people, and eventually for AI. pages.title: SPORT Mobile Cards — José Luis Pizarro
pages.headline: Product thought the cards were too tall. I started by measuring them.
pages.description: I measured 279 SPORT news cards to test whether they were too tall — and what compressing them would cost. Product Design, research and data.

sections.title: “Are these cards simply too tall?”
sections.text: At SPORT there was a strong product culture around the first scroll and how much editorial content a user sees on mobile. The concern was that the current news cards were consuming too much vertical space. Instead of starting from a redesign, I turned the concern into measurable criteria: text height, image height and whether cropping damaged the informational meaning of the photograph. RESEARCH MODEL / MOBILE CARDS 279 production cards measurable criteria 279 Type A cards 51 Type B cards 3 front pages 2 image ratios Criterion 01 Text density Does text cross the defined height threshold? Criterion 02 Image relationship Does text extend beyond the image height? Criterion 03 Editorial framing Does cropping preserve the informational meaning of the photograph?

sections.title: The target was not a shorter card. It was a better argument.
sections.text: The two get confused easily, so it is worth separating them before any number appears. What I set out to change How the decision got made. Product held a firm view about card height and there was no shared way to test it, so what I was after was a vocabulary — text height, image height, whether the crop destroys the meaning of the photograph — that anyone could argue with using evidence instead of taste. What I deliberately did not do Start from a redesign. Compression was the proposed answer, not the problem. Opening with a shorter card would have settled by opinion the exact question the measurement existed to open.

sections.title: I did the measuring. I did not do it in a vacuum.
sections.text: The benchmark, the criteria and the measurement were mine — that part is in the fact sheet and I will stand behind it. What surrounded them was not. A study like this is only worth running if its output has somewhere to land, and these are the people it landed with. Juan Francisco Molinera Product Design Lead LinkedIn Susana Cabado Design System Engineer LinkedIn Tania Domínguez Design, and Figma support through the study LinkedIn

sections.title: Define the problem before changing the component.
sections.text: I benchmarked other editorial brands and digital products, then measured the production card against explicit criteria. The Type A sample used the existing 1:1 image proportion with a 140px minimum height across three SPORT front pages. 279 news cards 3 front pages 1:1 production image ratio 140px minimum image height

sections.title: The concern was real — but “smaller” was not automatically “better”.
sections.text: The report documented that 86% of the analysed cards crossed the defined text-height threshold. In 40.86% of the total sample, text extended beyond the image height. At the same time, 81.88% of images were considered to retain an acceptable or meaningful framing. 86% of the cards exceeded the defined height threshold in Type A 279 cards analysed · one dot per card Within threshold Exceeded threshold One dot per production card, 279 in all, from the three SPORT front pages sampled. 240 of them crossed the text-height threshold: the 86% the report documented. Type A · Production What the sample revealed Percent of analysed cards 86% Text exceeds threshold 40.86% Text exceeds image height 81.88% Image framing retained The useful finding was not “make the card shorter”. It was that content density, readability and editorial image value were pulling in different directions.

sections.title: Test a 16:9 image without assuming the trade-off.
sections.text: I created a Type B alternative using a 16:9 image and no minimum image height, then tested 51 cards using comparable criteria. Image 1:1 Kicker Headline across the card Author TYPE A Image 16:9 Kicker Headline across the card Author TYPE B In this second sample, 100% of images were judged to keep an acceptable informational framing, although the text crossed the midpoint of the card in every case, with an average excess of 29.26%.

sections.title: The tighter card improved framing in the test — without removing the text-density question.
sections.text: Criterion 2 Images retaining meaningful framing Type A vs Type B 81.88% Type A · 1:1 100% Type B · 16:9 Important: the samples and layouts were different — 279 production cards against 51 in the alternative. The chart communicates the documented criterion inside each test; it is not a conversion or causal claim.

sections.title: The alternative did not stay an alternative.
sections.text: The 16:9 card was adopted. And the criteria that came out of the study — height, text density, framing — fed into the news card in 42DS, one of the core patterns of the system, which is what made the change consistent across the group instead of local to one front page. It also changed how the decision got made, which was the actual target: Product gained a shared way to discuss card height, text density and image meaning, with the evidence attached to each trade-off. The goal was never to make cards smaller at any cost. It was to understand what we gain — and what we risk losing — when we compress editorial content. See the system the card lives in

sections.title: Measure the assumption before polishing the answer.
sections.text: This project reinforced a habit that now shapes how I approach Product Design: translate subjective concerns into observable criteria, make the trade-offs visible and let the evidence improve the quality of the design conversation. pages.title: Interactive Media Map — José Luis Pizarro
pages.headline: The brief was simple: reproduce the map. The real problem wasn’t.
pages.description: A map that lived inside a JPEG. I replaced it with a Leaflet and IGN build maintained from a spreadsheet, so a location became a row to edit instead of a pixel to redraw.

sections.title: The requested interface was not the real problem.
sections.text: The previous solution was a set of static images: hard to maintain, poorly adapted to mobile, and impossible to update without opening an image editor. The request that reached me was, in essence, to draw it again. I proposed replacing what sat underneath it instead.

sections.title: The map itself is the evidence.
sections.text: This standalone view keeps the original Leaflet implementation, IGN tiles, real marker data, publication-specific icons, popups and Spain-wide bounds logic. I removed the surrounding newspaper chrome so the development is easier to inspect. Crónicas Prensa Ibérica / Leaflet + IGN Interactive development Original locations + custom publication markers Pan · zoom · popup

sections.title: Nobody set a bar, because nobody had asked for this.
sections.text: Worth saying plainly, because it is the part a case study usually invents afterwards. What was agreed Nothing was. The brief was to reproduce the existing map; replacing the solution underneath it was my call, and no one sets a target for work they have not commissioned. What I built against instead The two failures the old asset already had: it could not be updated without a designer, and it did not work on a phone. Those were the only reference points available, so they became the criteria.

sections.title: An interactive map, without adding a paid mapping platform.
sections.text: That requirement came from my design lead, not from me: the map could not become a running cost for the company. Google Maps and its equivalents were off the table, so the implementation had to stand on open technology: Leaflet, over IGN mapping resources. What the constraint bought No licence, no vendor and no per-view cost. The map could ship and keep running without opening a budget line, which is what made it approvable at all. What it cost Clustering, geocoding and routing arrive free with a paid platform; on Leaflet you build them or you go without. And the bill moved from a licence to my hours. The saving was real. The work was not free.

sections.title: The constraints came from the design lead. The solution did not.
sections.text: The split is worth stating, because it is what makes the rest of this case readable. Juan Francisco Molinera briefed me on the state the previous map was in, set the guidelines it had to respect — including that it could not become a running cost for the company — and opened the internal doors I needed to recover the data. Everything downstream of that was mine: proposing a different solution instead of redrawing the old one, the data model, the interaction and the integration with 42DS. Juan Francisco Molinera Product Design Lead — the brief, the guidelines the map had to respect, and the internal contacts for the data LinkedIn Editorial and business contacts Media names, geolocation and company data, held across different newsrooms

sections.title: Before the map, there had to be reliable data.
sections.text: The information was fragmented across editorial teams and nowhere in a usable shape. I assembled it myself in a spreadsheet — locations, media types, relationships and the fields the interface would need — and moved maintenance onto Google Sheets and CSV instead of image editing. Every location became a row of four fields instead of a pixel somebody had to redraw. Before A picture of the data mapa-medios-v7-FINAL.jpg · 1440×900 Moving one location means reopening the artwork and re-exporting. 82 locations, not one of them addressable. Same locations different maintenance model After The data itself locations.csv · 82 rows · IGN tiles Each location is a row. 16 mastheads · 13 regions · updated without touching the build. Country and province geometry: Instituto Geográfico Nacional, CC BY 4.0, via es-atlas.

sections.title: Use AI to extend execution capability, not to avoid product decisions.
sections.text: My background was design and CSS, not JavaScript at this level of complexity. AI support let me implement an interactive experience more complex than anything I had shipped alone, while the product structure, the data model, the behaviour and the 42DS integration stayed mine. The distinction matters: the decisions that were hard on this project are not the ones a model makes for you.

sections.title: Make maintenance part of the design.
sections.text: Editorial maintenance was expected to sit with the newsrooms. Because the data workflow was cheap enough to operate, Product could absorb that work when newsroom resources were short — and did. A decision about file formats ended up deciding who does the job.

sections.title: The data model outlived the map it was built for.
sections.text: Two things came out of it. Product took over editorial maintenance of the map, which is the outcome the previous decision existed to make possible. And the pattern travelled: syx--emotional-spain-map is a public, live project built on the same shape — a JSON file of coordinates and fields driving a Leaflet map, with the data as the thing you edit rather than the drawing. Different subject, same decision.

sections.title: Interaction work stopped being an exception.
sections.text: This is the project where building the interaction, and not just specifying it, became something I could take on; it is now a regular part of what I ship, in 42DS and in my own projects. What I would keep is the order — the data model before the interface. What I would change is that I replaced the solution without agreeing what success would mean. It worked out because maintainability turned out to be what everyone wanted, and that was not something I had established beforehand. pages.headline: World Cup 2026 — Building the experience I designed.
pages.description: I wrote the brief, the limits and the acceptance criteria before the first line of code, and published them alongside it. An interactive World Cup explorer built on SYX with GSAP, Three.js and Leaflet.

sections.title: SYX could only show itself, and that proves nothing.
sections.text: The system had documentation, a token showcase and a page explaining its own architecture — all of it about SYX. A design system is not proved by describing itself. It is proved by carrying a product where it is the means and not the subject. What I wanted to find out was whether SYX could hold an editorial project with more visual ambition than anything it had carried before.

sections.title: Eleven documents before the first line.
sections.text: Scope, screens, data layer, motion and 3D guidelines, theming, build rules — and two that mattered more than the rest: the boundaries and the acceptance criteria. They live in the repository, dated, and anyone can open them. That is the whole point of publishing them. On a self-directed project nobody can tell whether the brief came before the result or after it, unless the brief is public. 00-project-overview What the product is and who it is for 01-strategy-and-boundaries What the project must be, and what it must never be 02-syx-architecture-mandatory-rules The architecture rules the build is not allowed to break 03-design-system-application How SYX maps onto this particular product 04-product-scope-and-screens The MVP views and the purpose of each one 05-data-sources-and-data-layer Public feeds, and the normalisation layer between them and the interface…

sections.title: I work in sports media. I was building a World Cup product on my own time.
sections.kicker: The line I had to draw
sections.text: That is a conflict waiting to be misread, so the rules went in writing before anything else did. What the project had to be A public-data editorial explorer and a showcase for the design system, running on legitimate open feeds. Editorial in tone, exploratory in structure, and open about being a portfolio piece. What it could not be, under any reading No betting, no porra, no predictor, no fantasy, no leaderboards. No naming that resembles a newsroom product label, no internal or private data, and no implication of insider strategy of any kind.

sections.title: The work was coordinating three libraries, not adding them.
sections.text: GSAP for motion, Leaflet for the map, Three.js as a focused accent layer, across eight screens on Vite and Sass. Dropping any one of the three into a page is easy. Making them share a single interaction language across eight screens, inside the token and component rules SYX already imposes, is where the project actually was. There was no team on this one: the eleven documents were the only thing keeping me honest. AI accelerated the implementation — the intent, the limits and the system were already written down.

sections.title: I wrote twenty-eight acceptance criteria and never went back to them.
sections.kicker: The bar, and what I did with it
sections.text: The checklist covers eight areas: architecture, how visible SYX is in the result, product framing, the data layer, motion, multitheming, delivery, and a final pass. I wrote it as part of the brief and I never ran it as a closing review. It did deliver something — while I was building, it kept deciding what the project was allowed to be. What it did not deliver is the thing it was designed for. A checklist with no date in the calendar is documentation, not control. Specifications 11 Acceptance criteria 28 Screens shipped 8 Counted in project-docs and in the built screens of the public repository on 22 August 2026. First commit, 7 March 2026.

sections.title: A closed piece, and the one I open when someone asks how far I go.
sections.text: The repository has not moved since March and does not need to: this is a finished piece, not a product with a roadmap. What it does now is answer one question faster than any description of it — how far past the hand-off this actually goes. That is the job it has.

sections.title: The system holds at a higher visual register than its own documentation.
sections.text: What I set out to check was whether SYX could serve an editorial project with real visual ambition — motion, 3D, mapping, several themes — without the architecture giving way underneath it. It could, and that is the answer I keep. What I would change is the part I already know about: the criteria were written and the review was never scheduled, so the project was governed at the start and ungoverned at the end. pages.title: ATLAS × SYX — AI-governed editorial system · José Luis Pizarro
pages.headline: Giving AI a system to think and build with.
pages.description: ATLAS layers editorial intent on top of SYX so AI-assisted long-form experiences can vary creatively without abandoning technical governance.
pages.kicker: Case study 05 · Self-directed · AI-native editorial system · 2026

sections.title: SYX governs how a page is built. Nothing governed what it should say.
sections.text: SYX is my design system: tokens, accessibility, architecture, a validator that fails the build. It answers how something is built. It holds no opinion about editorial hierarchy, about the distance between a portrait and a dossier, about when a page should feel slow. I wanted to know whether that second body of rules could be generated separately — as its own system, with its own vocabulary — and whether SYX would take orders from it. ATLAS is that second system. Digital media is the domain I used to test it.

sections.title: Two opposite registers, one system.
sections.text: I wrote the bar down before starting, so that the result could not quietly move it. What I set out to prove Two long-form experiences sharing the semantic API and disagreeing on everything else — typography, palette, motion, tension — built without editing SYX and without lowering the accessibility floor. What would have counted as failure One register, or two that differed only in colour. A system that produces one thing is not a system, it is a template.

sections.title: Two registers, and a media budget I would not accept in production.
sections.text: Two deliberate constraints, and I would rather name the price than leave it out. What the constraint bought Two registers far enough apart to be worth comparing, and a motion language taken to its ceiling instead of to a safe midpoint. The test needed both extremes to mean anything. What it cost Two registers prove variation, not that the semantic API scales — that would take a fourth and a fifth. And the pieces carry a media budget that is indefensible in a client product: 14.6 MB and 52.9 MB of video. ATELIER · declared media 17 MB OBSIDIANA · declared media 57 MB Registers built 2 Sum of the declared external assets of both published pages, measured on 22 August 2026. Not a simulated page load: video is served progressively, so a first visit transfers less. Act 02 How the rules were built

sections.title: Knowledge split into domains, loaded on demand.
sections.kicker: The decision the project hangs from
sections.text: I broke the rules into six domains that load separately, inside a public mind-system of 340 files, so a task reads only the domain it needs instead of the whole body of rules. Everything else follows from that. Splitting the knowledge is what makes a second system cheap enough to consult on every single task, and a second system nobody consults is documentation, not governance. branding Perception of prestige: foundations, and the rules derived from them front Accessibility, CSS architecture, semantics, progressive enhancement motion Ten patterns, plus fundamentals, capabilities and a glossary syx Tokens, themes, OKLCH colour and the SCSS pipeline ui Typography systems, colour theory, practical interface craft ux Heuristics, laws of UX, microinteractions, writing for interfaces

sections.title: ATLAS decides what the experience should feel like. SYX decides how it is built.
sections.text: ATLAS is the editorial mental model; SYX is the executor. The split keeps creative direction from leaking into implementation rules, and it is what makes the stack debuggable: when a piece comes out wrong, it is an intent problem or a build problem, and the two live in different repositories. ATLAS Editorial intent ↓ ATELIER OBSIDIANA ↓ SYX · governed execution tokens · accessibility · motion patterns · architecture

sections.title: Ten motion patterns became part of the system, not part of a prompt.
sections.text: The motion domain documents ten reusable patterns — narrative intent, parameters, GSAP controls, the prompt that invokes each one and the reduced-motion fallback it degrades to. A pattern written into the system is loaded by a mode; a pattern described in a prompt is rediscovered on every task. That is the whole distance between context and instruction. character-cascade Letters enter one after another cursor-follower A mark that trails the pointer draw-svg-path A line that draws itself horizontal-scroll Vertical scroll moved sideways magnetic-button A control that pulls toward the pointer mask-reveal Content uncovered by a moving mask parallax Layers travelling at different depths pinned-scrub A pinned section scrubbed by scroll position scramble-text Characters resolving into words typewriter Text typed out on entry Act 03 What it proved

sections.title: Same system. Two radically different editorial registers.
sections.text: ATELIER and OBSIDIANA are rendered directly from the published GitHub Pages experiences. The previews are intentionally non-interactive here; each project can be opened separately to explore the full motion and scroll behaviour. ATELIER Open live ATELIER Live preview unavailable — open project Cinematic profiles Human · editorial · motion-led OBSIDIANA Open live OBSIDIANA Live preview unavailable — open project Forensic dossiers Data · investigation · controlled tension

sections.title: Thirty-two shared semantic tokens. Three shared primitives.
sections.text: Whether two pages look alike is an opinion, so I counted instead. ATELIER declares 35 semantic tokens and OBSIDIANA declares 37; 32 of those names are the same. Underneath them ATELIER declares 15 primitives and OBSIDIANA 14, and only 3 are shared. The two pieces speak an almost identical semantic API on top of almost entirely different identity values — which is the behaviour the stack was built to produce, stated as something a reader can go and recount. Shared semantic tokens 32 Shared primitives 3 Knowledge domains 6 Custom properties declared in the two published pages, counted by name on 22 August 2026. Both files are served from the same repository. Act 04 What it left behind

sections.title: The method moved to a domain with nothing editorial about it.
sections.text: ATLAS was not absorbed into SYX — the traffic ran the other way, and SYX is untouched by it. What travelled was the shape: a domain system sitting on an execution system, with the knowledge split into loadable domains. SYX-mail applies that shape to HTML email, where the constraints are Outlook and Gmail instead of editorial hierarchy: a mental model, six knowledge domains, one mode. This portfolio runs on it too — eight domain skills over a router that decides which ones a task loads. Neither of them is about media, and that is the part that makes the test worth something.

sections.title: Writing the pattern down costs more than writing the code.
sections.text: Documenting the ten motion patterns took longer than implementing them would have taken in the two pieces that use them. Written knowledge only pays back above a certain number of pieces, and I did not know that number when I started — I still don’t. So the honest reading of this project is narrower than the ambition behind it: it shows that two systems compose, not that writing the second one down was the cheaper route. pages.title: SPORT Illustrations — Editorial illustration · José Luis Pizarro
pages.headline: SPORT Illustrations — Building character without breaking the product language.
pages.description: Seventeen original illustrations for SPORT, held together by one visual grammar: silhouette, palette, editorial humour and reusable placement.

sections.title: It started as one asset, not as a set.
sections.text: The first one was a one-off: a product moment that needed an image and did not have one. Then another moment needed one, and then another. At some point the question stopped being what this particular drawing should look like and became what all of them had to have in common. That is when a handful of illustrations turns into something worth solving properly, and it is also when it becomes possible to get it wrong at scale.

sections.title: Seventeen assets, one grammar.
sections.text: Each one answers a specific product moment — a survey, a failed process, a subscription, a match day — with the same silhouette, the same palette and the same register of humour. 01 Social media 02 Euro 2024 03 Permanent subscription 04 Newsletter 05 Survey 06 Comments 07 Tennis 08 Discount 09 Club benefits 10 Subscriber benefits 11 Failed process 12 Print edition 13 Puzzles 14 Halloween 15 Completed process 16 Football 17 Registered-user benefits 17 assets Original SVG The complete set, at the same scale and on the same baseline. Numbering follows the order shown here, not a chronology.

sections.title: The set grew because someone kept asking for the next one.
sections.text: I drew them, but I did not decide when the set needed to grow. Deborah Garcelán Vargas, then at SPORT, reviewed each illustration with me and told me which one was missing next as communication needs came up. That is why the seventeen cover the moments they cover: the list was never designed in advance, it was requested one piece at a time. It is also why the grammar could only be written at the end — you cannot extract the rules of a set while the set is still being asked for. Deborah Garcelán Vargas SPORT at the time — reviewed every illustration and asked for the new ones as communication needs appeared LinkedIn

sections.title: Distinctive enough to have character. Flexible enough to live inside a product.
sections.text: The set covers different editorial and product needs — sport, engagement, newsletter, subscription and utility contexts — without turning every asset into a separate visual universe.

sections.title: Three limits, and all three are visible in the drawings.
sections.text: None of them was mine to negotiate, and the set looks the way it looks because of them. What I worked inside SPORT is a photographic newspaper and its palette was already fixed. The illustration could not compete with the photography for attention, and it could not invent colour to tell one asset apart from another. What that cost A quieter register than I would have chosen, and less separation between assets than a free palette would have given me. They were also drawn around other work rather than in time set aside for them, which puts a ceiling on how far any single one got pushed.

sections.title: Variation comes from scenario. Consistency comes from the visual grammar.
sections.text: I did not decide these four rules and then draw. I drew, then looked at what the drawings already had in common, and wrote that down. The order matters more than it sounds: a grammar extracted from work that exists describes something real, while one declared in advance is a wish. These four are what let a Halloween asset and a failed-process asset belong to the same family. 01 Recognisable silhouette Simple, bold forms keep the asset legible at editorial scale. 02 Controlled palette Colour reinforces SPORT identity without overwhelming the surrounding UI. 03 Editorial humour Small narrative gestures make functional moments feel less generic. 04 Reusable placement Assets can work as standalone illustrations, empty states or contextual support.

sections.title: Some of them have been retired, and that was always going to happen.
sections.text: A set that holds Euro 2024 and Halloween next to a failed-process state has two different lifespans built into it from the start. The ones tied to a moment have gone. The ones tied to a permanent product state are the reason the grammar had to exist in the first place: an empty state does not stop being needed. That split is visible in the sheet above once you look for it, and it is the part of the brief nobody writes down.

sections.title: Systems thinking should make visual expression easier to scale — not flatten it.
sections.text: The grammar is what makes seventeen assets readable as one set; the scenarios are what keep them from looking like seventeen copies. Previous case ← ATLAS × SYX Back Selected work Questions about this project? Get in touch
